# How to use this guide

Study one unit, solve its representative problem, and only then attempt the final quiz. The sequence follows the conceptual dependencies in the 3Blue1Brown _Essence of Linear Algebra_ playlist.

# Unit 1 — Vectors, combinations, and bases

A vector is an ordered list of scalars:

$$
\mathbf v=\begin{bmatrix}v_1\\v_2\\\vdots\\v_n\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The essential operations are

$$
\mathbf u+\mathbf v=\begin{bmatrix}u_1+v_1\\u_2+v_2\end{bmatrix},
\qquad c\mathbf v=\begin{bmatrix}cv_1\\cv_2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

A linear combination has the form

$$
c_1\mathbf v_1+\cdots+c_k\mathbf v_k.
$$

A basis is a linearly independent spanning set. Coordinates tell us which linear combination of the basis vectors produces a vector.

## Representative problem

Find (a,b) such that

$$
a\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\end{bmatrix}+b\begin{bmatrix}2\\-1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}7\\1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

# Unit 2 — Linear transformations and matrices

A transformation (T) is linear when

$$
T(\mathbf u+\mathbf v)=T(\mathbf u)+T(\mathbf v),
\qquad T(c\mathbf v)=cT(\mathbf v).
$$

Every linear transformation can be written as

$$
T(\mathbf x)=A\mathbf x.
$$

The columns of (A) are the images of the standard basis vectors. Matrix multiplication is composition:

$$
(AB)\mathbf x=A(B\mathbf x).
$$

For a (2\times2) matrix,

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{bmatrix},
\qquad \det(A)=ad-bc.
$$

The matrix is invertible exactly when its determinant is nonzero.

## Representative problem

For

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\0&3\end{bmatrix},
$$

compute (A[1,2]^T), (det(A)), and decide whether (A) is invertible.

# Unit 3 — Systems, dot products, and cross products

A linear system is represented by

$$
A\mathbf x=\mathbf b.
$$

The dot product is

$$
\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=\sum_i u_iv_i=\|\mathbf u\|\|\mathbf v\|\cos\theta.
$$

Perpendicular vectors have dot product zero.

In three dimensions,

$$
\mathbf u\times\mathbf v=
\begin{bmatrix}
u_2v_3-u_3v_2\\
u_3v_1-u_1v_3\\
u_1v_2-u_2v_1
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The cross product is perpendicular to both inputs, and

$$
\|\mathbf u\times\mathbf v\|=\|\mathbf u\|\|\mathbf v\|\sin\theta.
$$

## Representative problem

For (mathbf u=[1,2,0]^T) and (mathbf v=[2,-1,1]^T), compute (mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v) and (mathbf u\times\mathbf v).

# Unit 4 — Determinants, basis changes, and eigenvalues

Important determinant identities are

$$
\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B),
\qquad \det(A^{-1})=\frac1{\det(A)}.
$$

Eigenvectors satisfy

$$
A\mathbf v=\lambda\mathbf v,
\qquad \mathbf v\ne\mathbf0.
$$

Eigenvalues solve the characteristic equation

$$
\det(A-\lambda I)=0.
$$

If (A) has enough independent eigenvectors, then

$$
A=PDP^{-1},
\qquad A^n=PD^nP^{-1}.
$$

For a (2\times2) matrix,

$$
\lambda_1+\lambda_2=\operatorname{tr}(A),
\qquad \lambda_1\lambda_2=\det(A).
$$

## Representative problem

Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}3&1\\0&2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

# Unit 5 — Abstract vector spaces

Vectors need not be arrows: polynomials, matrices, functions, and sequences can also form vector spaces. For the polynomial basis

$$
\mathcal B=\{1,x,x^2\},
$$

the polynomial (p(x)=4-2x+3x^2) has coordinate vector

$$
[p]_{\mathcal B}=\begin{bmatrix}4\\-2\\3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The same ideas—span, independence, basis, coordinates, and linear transformations—apply in every vector space.

## Representative problem

Express (p(x)=2+5x-x^2) in coordinates relative to

$$
\mathcal B=\{1+x,x,x^2\}.
$$

# Quiz

Attempt these closed-notes first. Each question is worth 2 points.

1. Find (a,b) such that (a[1,2]^T+b[2,-1]^T=[7,1]^T).
2. State the two conditions a set must satisfy to be a basis.
3. Find the matrix for (T(x,y)=(x+2y,3x-y)).
4. Compute
   $$
   \begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2\\1\end{bmatrix}.
   $$
5. Solve (x+y=5) and (2x-y=1).
6. Are ([1,2,3]^T) and ([2,-1,0]^T) perpendicular?
7. Compute ([1,0,1]^T\times[2,1,0]^T).
8. Find the determinant of ([\begin{smallmatrix}4&2\\1&3\end{smallmatrix}]).
9. Find the eigenvalues of ([\begin{smallmatrix}4&1\\0&2\end{smallmatrix}]).
10. Express (2+5x-x^2) in the basis ({1+x,x,x^2}).
11. Explain why matrix multiplication represents composition of transformations.
12. Explain why the determinant being zero prevents invertibility.

## Scoring

- 20–24: ready for a cumulative problem set.
- 14–19: review the missed units and retry.
- 0–13: work through the representative problems slowly, then retake the quiz.

The [answer key](answer.qmd) gives worked solutions.
